THE HOW & THE WHY

Plan the time. Explore the trip.

Two planners answer different questions: will the current help or slow my passage? and how much tide will there be when I reach the places that matter? This guide walks through both.

The start and finish choices select a stretch of an existing course. These pages do not generate a new navigable route, select a marina berth, or add a detour to a dock. A named town or inlet is a passage position on that course.

Use the map without losing your place

  1. Zoom with the mouse wheel over the map. Drag to pan. On touch devices, use a two-finger pinch or the map’s zoom controls.
  2. Rotate in 45° steps. The left and right rotation buttons turn the map; North up resets the orientation. The orientation label tells you which way north points.
  3. Pick your endpoints. Use the Start and Finish dropdowns, or press that field’s Pick on map button. The button changes to Cancel picking. Click a named waypoint, or click nearby to select the nearest named endpoint. An arbitrary click does not create a new waypoint. Pick a different start and finish; a valid map selection recalculates automatically.
  4. Inspect the passage. When endpoint picking is off, click along the route, a station, or a table row. At this point updates immediately. The Explore along the route slider does the same thing in travel order.
  5. Navigate from a list. Click a geographic bridge, prediction point, Coast Guard notice, passage stop or waypoint in a location list, briefing or endpoint dropdown. The map pans smoothly to it and a ring highlights the point until you select another location. The ring keeps pulsing on the inset map and stays visible on the full map after its initial pulse. Zoom, rotation, route colors and other markers remain in place. Selecting a location does not scroll the page to the map. Existing map markers still open their usual inspection or notice details. Selected location rows in both planners stay highlighted when you move to the map, pan or zoom, or recalculate the same passage. Matching current-station entries in the lists and briefing share the highlight. Selecting another location moves it. Geographic rows also support Enter or Space; notices without coordinates show their details without moving the map.
  6. Use the floating map preview. If the main map is offscreen, a larger live map preview appears in the lower-right corner with your selected point centered at the same zoom and orientation. Hold the left mouse button and drag the preview to pan. Use the mouse wheel to zoom in or out; the page stays in place, and the main map keeps your pan position, zoom and rotation when it returns. The inset stays open while your pointer is over it, including its buttons. After you move away, it closes in about four seconds unless you return or select another location. Panning and wheel zoom also keep it open. Click the Return to full map button or an empty part of the preview to scroll smoothly to the main map. Dragging does not trigger a return. Markers keep their normal inspection behavior. Use × to dismiss the preview. It also closes after inactivity or when you scroll the main map back into view. No preview appears when the main map is already visible. Movement and highlighting respect your reduced-motion preference.
  7. Compare departure times at the same location. Click the departure comparison graph to choose a sampled departure. The location you are inspecting stays selected, while its arrival time and current or tide change. The map’s zoom and position stay put.

Press Show whole route when you deliberately want to fit the selected passage to the screen. Recalculation preserves your map view. Deliberately selecting a geographic location pans to that point while preserving zoom and rotation. Changing the start or finish can reset the inspected trip position because it is a different passage.

NOAA nautical chart loads chart tiles separately over the internet. Zoom in to see available soundings and navigation marks. Simple coastline uses saved land shapes and is helpful if the chart service is slow. It has no soundings. Map colors describe predictions at your arrival time, not a single snapshot of conditions everywhere.

Current planner: step by step

This planner is especially useful for sailboats and other slower boats: a few knots of current can make a large difference to speed over ground and passage time. Faster powerboats can use it too, but the current usually represents a smaller share of their cruising speed.

  1. Enter the departure date and time. All input and displayed times use Eastern time, with daylight saving applied. The page shows the saved date range.
  2. Select Start and Finish. Choose the portion of the coast you want to travel. ⇅ Swap reverses the passage.
  3. Set Boat information before Passage options. The highlighted speed section sits immediately above Passage options. The initial 6 knots is an example; enter your boat’s cruising speed through water before using the passage estimates. Use the boat’s expected speed in still water, not a GPS speed already helped or hindered by current. The current planner holds this speed constant; it does not model no-wake slowdowns or bridge waits.
  4. Review the selected departure. Valid input changes recalculate automatically; you can also press Calculate passage. The selected card shows the full weekday, date, time and EST or EDT designation for the actual departure used in the calculation, followed by time underway and arrival. The other cards identify the fastest and slowest completed passages in the comparison window.
  5. Explore a place that matters. Click the route near Hell Gate or the Race, for example. Read arrival time, current speed, current direction, following/opposing component and speed over ground in At this point.
  6. Try a different departure. Click the comparison graph or a Use best/worst departure button. Watch the values change at your selected location. Open Waypoint arrivals to see the trip unfold at the main endpoints.
Example: timing the Race

The route now passes through NOAA’s The Race current prediction station (LIS1001, bin 13), at 41.22818° N, 72.06252° W, south-southwest of Race Point on Fishers Island. This replaces the former point closer to Fishers Island, which skirted the main Race crossing. NOAA station details.

Select a passage through The Race · NOAA current station and click that waypoint on the map. Change departures on the comparison graph while watching At this point: your arrival time, current speed and direction, and following or opposing component update at the same location. This lets you explore a favorable current or a time near slack at the Race.

The fastest-departure recommendation minimizes the duration of the whole selected passage; it does not specifically target slack water at the Race. Inspect that crossing yourself when its timing is your main concern. The station prediction describes one location and depth, not the strongest current everywhere in the Race or the effects of wind and waves.

Read the departure comparison

The horizontal axis is departure time; the vertical axis is total time underway. Lower is faster. The search samples every ten minutes from ten hours before to ten hours after the departure entered when the trip was last recalculated. It can cross midnight and includes nighttime departures.

Fastest means shortest passage duration. It does not mean earliest clock-time arrival or best weather. Choosing a graph result keeps that original comparison window. Changing a trip input or pressing Calculate centers a new window on the entered departure time. Departures the model cannot complete are excluded; the note below the graph reports them.

Read the current map

Following and opposing colors describe the component of current along your course at the estimated arrival. Near slack means very little modeled current. Arrows point in the direction the water flows, in true degrees. A cross-current can reduce forward speed even when the along-course component is favorable. Gray means current is unmodeled, particularly on the offshore New Jersey legs; it does not mean slack water.

How current timing works

The boat advances along the course in steps of at most one minute. At each step the planner evaluates saved NOAA current predictions at the boat’s changing position and time. Nearby station current vectors are blended along modeled course segments. The calculation accounts for following, opposing and cross-current, assuming the boat steers to stay on the course.

Harmonic station data are saved at six-minute intervals. Subordinate stations use smooth estimates between predicted slack and maximum-current events. Station depths and sources appear under Sources, station depths & calculation assumptions; a station’s prediction depth is not the depth of water under your boat.

A passage is rejected if the model cannot maintain forward progress or exceeds 120 hours. Unmodeled segments use the entered boat speed without a current adjustment. Wind, waves, river discharge, traffic, stops and actual throttle changes are outside this calculation.

Tide planner: step by step

  1. Enter the departure date and Eastern time. Choose either northbound or southbound travel. The dropdowns run north to south, with Manasquan Inlet first and Cape May last.
  2. Choose the route, Start and Finish. The tide planner starts on Stay inside each time you open it. Choose an ocean alternative for the current visit when needed. Saved boat settings remain available. Stops include the LBI passage points, Barnegat Inlet’s nearby ICW junction, Atlantic City, Ocean City, Sea Isle, Avalon and Stone Harbor. A shortened passage checks only the priority checkpoints along that stretch.
  3. Set Boat information before Passage options. The section starts expanded so you can check inside and ocean cruising speeds first. The starting 26-knot speeds are examples; arrival tide estimates depend on your boat’s passage timing. Use the arrow beside Boat information to collapse or reopen the section. Your values stay in place when it is collapsed. Maximum height is your boat’s highest point above the current waterline, including antennas and equipment in the configuration you will actually use. It selects bridge openings and waits. Add an extra clearance margin (default 2 feet). Draft is saved for a future depth feature and does not affect the calculation.
  4. Set your low-water alert level. The default is 1.0 foot above MLLW. Change it to the tide height you want flagged. It is a planning alert level, not a minimum navigable depth.
  5. Set bridge delays. Albany and Dorset default to expected waits from their published schedules and your arrival time; choose Manual slider to use an assumed wait. Other movable bridges start at 15 minutes, adjustable from 0 to 30. With height entered, only an indicated opening or an unchecked movable crossing adds its wait. Fixed bridges and estimated closed passes add no wait.
  6. Results update automatically. Changing the date, time, endpoints, cruise speed, boat dimensions or bridge settings recalculates arrival tides and recommendations. Pause briefly after typing; no Calculate button is needed. Your map zoom and position stay unchanged. Check the selected departure card, low-water notice and six-checkpoint table. Each checkpoint uses its own arrival time.
  7. Compare departures. Use the best tide window button or click the graph. Keep a spot selected on the map to watch its arrival tide change. Review bridge arrivals and the full station table for details.
Example: leaving Cape May at 1 p.m.

The planner first estimates your arrival at Wildwood Crest, then Nummy Island, Ludlam Bay, Ocean City, Beesleys Point near red 280, Great Thoroughfare at Atlantic City near G207 and Main Marsh, in northbound travel order. Those are six different tide times. A longer Margate wait shifts the Great Thoroughfare checkpoint and Main Marsh arrivals later; it does not shift places you have already passed.

At this point shows estimated tide in feet MLLW, rising/falling water level, next high and low tide, arrival time, elapsed time and the timing section. Rising or falling describes water level; it is not a current direction. A dashed connector identifies the prediction source used for a nearby-station estimate.

Gold labeled markers identify the six priority checkpoints. A red outline flags a priority checkpoint below your alert level. Route colors give a broader estimate blended between nearby tide sources. Use the checkpoint table to read the actual values used for ranking and alerts.

Low-water alerts & best departure

For each candidate departure, the planner computes the estimated tide at each included priority checkpoint’s individual arrival. It then takes the lowest of those heights. The best departure maximizes that lowest value; the lowest tide window minimizes it. The graph’s vertical axis is this minimum in feet MLLW, so higher gives the larger modeled tide margin across your checkpoints.

The alert compares each arrival estimate against Flag arrival tide below. Equality is at the alert level; only values below it trigger the warning. The notice names all flagged checkpoints, and the table labels each one. Changing the alert level updates the notice and markers immediately, without changing the route timing or recommendation ranking.

The best departure can still have a low-water alert: it is the best among the sampled departures, not a promise that all six have enough water. Check the selected departure’s notice after choosing it. A passage with no priority checkpoint has no best/lowest tide recommendation, but the other station arrivals remain available.

These are on-page planning notices. They do not send texts or emails, monitor a live gauge, or notify you while the page is closed.

What MLLW means

Mean Lower Low Water is a tidal height reference used for many nautical chart depths. A tide of 1.2 ft MLLW is water level 1.2 feet above that datum; it does not say there are 1.2 feet of water at the checkpoint.

If a verified charted depth were 4.0 feet at MLLW, adding a predicted 1.2-foot tide would give a nominal 5.2-foot water column. This planner does not supply that verified depth or subtract draft, squat or a clearance margin. Wind and weather can move actual water levels away from astronomical predictions, especially in back bays.

Coast Guard notices on the map

Aids with explicit temporary-replacement codes (TRLB/TRUB) are hidden by default when their remaining codes describe the original missing, damaged or destroyed aid or associated hazard. Off-station, sinking, lighting and unspecified additional problems remain visible. Select Include aids with a reported temporary replacement to restore these records to the list and map. A temporary substitute does not change the original correction status or establish the replacement’s present condition.

Turn on Show Coast Guard notice markers & areas. Orange exclamation markers identify notices with point locations; click a marker to open the full notice, effective dates and source links. Geographic lines and areas are drawn where supplied. The notice list provides the same text, including District 5 notices without a precise location.

The page matches notices to the selected passage within a half-nautical-mile corridor by default (optionally 2 nautical miles), or where a notice area overlaps the route, and to the Eastern calendar dates between departure and final arrival. It uses notice start/end dates as supplied; read the text for work hours, conditions and exceptions. Changing trip endpoints, dates or timing updates the match automatically. District-wide notices without coordinates may apply more broadly than this route.

Aid discrepancies: headlines show the reported problem, with separate physical, lighting/visibility and other filters. Physical problems are selected by default; lighting and other reports remain selectable. Age filters do not remove aid records. Each aid counts once at its highest-priority problem; multiple source reports remain in expanded details. Correction status unreported means Status uncertain. Approved publication status does not establish that a defect is still outstanding. Explicit correction/cancellation information is labeled restored/canceled and can be included with its checkbox. Source file update, source record creation, and actual report/correction dates are kept distinct. A created date is not assumed to be the date the discrepancy occurred. Symbols are ▲ physical, ◐ visibility and ◆ other. Assigned/charted and explicitly observed positions are labeled separately when supplied; a generic source point is not treated as an observed off-station location.

Important & recent shows other notices reported or updated within 90 days. Aid discrepancies use their independent filters and remain available regardless of age. Longstanding shoaling uses its original effective/report date; a timestamp-only edit does not make it new. After a baseline snapshot, changes to notice text, geometry or effective dates are tracked separately. Existing explicit bridge restrictions stay visible. Routine proposals, administrative reviews and undated entries are hidden. Choose All active to include older and routine records. Missing dates are omitted from summaries rather than repeated as unknown.

A snapshot of supported NAVCEN geographic files is refreshed weekly with the existing Monday marine-data job. The source categories include bridge notices, hazards, construction, marine events, safety zones, marine safety bulletins, navigation changes and current federal/private aid discrepancies. The stored region covers the full NJ route with a five-nautical-mile bounding margin. Weekly PDF special notices and radio-only warnings are not automatically parsed. This layer does not promise complete notice coverage.

Coast Guard notices update automatically each week. Opening the planner loads the latest published data; an open page checks again every 30 minutes and when you return to it. No sign-in, refresh button or other user action is required.

The panel shows retrieval time and flags snapshots older than eight days. If some source files fail, the update is explicitly marked PARTIAL, names the number of unavailable files, retains their older records where available, and preserves the last-complete-refresh date. If all files fail, the previous snapshot and timestamp remain unchanged. A partial or stale update is not an all-clear. Loading the latest snapshot checks the published cache, not NAVCEN directly. Notices inform your planning but do not automatically change bridge opening rules, delays or clearance calculations.

Official Coast Guard NAVCEN Maritime Safety Information is the source. Check it for updates before traveling, including notices outside the supplied geographic files.

Bridge delays: height selects the crossings that matter

The full recorded passage crosses 23 reviewed bridge locations, counting Route 72’s parallel spans as one crossing. Fourteen are movable. The bridge table and delay controls follow your actual direction of travel.

Enter maximum boat height and an extra clearance margin in Boat information. Height and margin changes recalculate automatically. Albany and Dorset offer arrival-based schedule waits by default. Manual waits are adjustable from 0–30 minutes, default 15. An Opening indicated or Clearance needs check result applies that wait. An estimated closed pass or fixed bridge adds no wait. Without a boat height, all movable crossings are assumed to need openings and use their selected wait method; no clearance decision is made.

Outputs show the applied wait for the selected departure. In expected mode the slider is disabled and its saved manual setting is retained. An estimated closed pass moves its slider to zero, disables it, and explains that an opening is not required. Your opening-wait setting is retained separately and returns if a different height or arrival tide requires an opening.

The departure comparison can jump when a bridge wait changes suddenly, especially when an arrival enters overnight advance-notice hours without notice arranged. These waits can shift priority-location arrivals into another tide cycle. The chart breaks its line across wait changes of an hour or more; hover for wait details. A best-tide departure with a long bridge wait states that wait on its card.

Albany Avenue + Dorset Avenue: arrival-based opening waits

Each bridge offers Expected from arrival & schedule or Manual slider. Expected mode uses the arrival date and Eastern time, including every earlier bridge wait. Arrive at Dorset at 10:14 a.m. in July and the timetable wait is 1 minute, to 10:15; arrive at 10:16 and it is 29 minutes, to 10:45. At an opening instant the wait is zero. Calculations retain seconds even though arrival tables display minutes; wait totals are rounded to a tenth of a minute. Expected waits may exceed the manual slider’s 30-minute maximum.

US 40–322 · Albany Avenue:00 / :30 from 9 a.m.–4 p.m. and 6–9 p.m.; closed 4–6 p.m.On signal otherwise, except four-hour notice is required year-round 11 p.m.–7 a.m. and November 1–March 31, 3–11 p.m.
Dorset Avenue:15 / :45 from 9:15 a.m.–9:15 p.m.On signal otherwise, except four-hour notice is required year-round 11 p.m.–7 a.m. (including the 2026 rule change).

Required four-hour notice already arranged is unchecked by default at each bridge. During notice-only hours, expected mode waits until the next regular service period. Check it only if you have actually arranged the required notice for your crossing; that enables an on-signal estimate during notice-only hours. Simply waiting four hours does not give notice. On-signal service contributes zero timetable wait; calling, bridge movement and maneuvering time are not included. Use the manual slider if you want to allow for those delays.

Albany’s July 4 closure from 9:40–11:15 p.m. is included. Its conditional July 5 fireworks rain date and the third-or-fourth Wednesday August air-show rule require confirmation of the actual event date. The planner flags affected arrivals, shows the saved manual wait as a fallback and excludes those departures from recommendations while expected mode is selected. Choose Manual slider after checking current notices. Temporary deviations and closures are not fetched automatically.

Coordinate Albany + Dorset applies only when both use Manual slider. If both need openings, it preserves the earlier one-wait assumption; the second adds no wait. When either bridge uses expected mode, coordination is disabled and each crossing is evaluated independently. Actual route timing determines whether you catch the offset opening. Boat-height checks still remove the wait for an estimated closed pass. With height blank or clearance unchecked, the selected wait method assumes an opening is needed.

Regular schedules checked October 21, 2026 against 33 CFR 117.733(h), Albany and 117.733(i), Dorset. These are published operating rules, not confirmation that an opening has been requested or that a bridge is currently available.

Arrival is before that bridge’s wait, including waits at upstream crossings. Clear bridge adds this crossing’s applied wait. Clearances are evaluated at arrival. A falling tide during a wait is not used to optimize a closed crossing; the scenario assumes an opening when indicated at arrival.

Select Only bridges needing opening / attention to narrow the map and table. Uncheck it to see all crossings, including fixed bridges. Click a bridge marker or row for the published height, estimated arrival clearance, tide source, height threshold and source link. Changing departure keeps the bridge selected and the map view in place.

A Fixed bridge too low result means its estimated clearance is below boat height plus margin. Those departure candidates are excluded from recommendations. If every sampled departure has a fixed-bridge conflict or incomplete data, the page keeps your selected scenario visible and reports no eligible departure. Bridge waits cannot solve a fixed-bridge conflict by opening it.

Manual sliders model assumed waits. Expected mode models only the published Albany and Dorset rules; neither mode guarantees an opening is available. Train movements, notice requirements, maintenance, temporary clearance reductions and actual bridge position are not automatically monitored. Check current USCG Maritime Safety Information and the posted bridge clearance boards.

Bridge clearances: MHW is not MLLW

The published bridge heights in NOAA Coast Pilot 3, chapter 5, page 198 (11 October 2026) are feet above mean high water (MHW). Our saved tide heights are feet above mean lower low water (MLLW). Subtracting an MLLW tide directly from a published MHW bridge height would mix two different references.

Estimated clearance at arrival

Published closed/fixed height + source MHW above source MLLW − predicted source tide at bridge arrival.

Maximum estimated tide for boat + margin

Published closed/fixed height + source MHW above source MLLW − boat height − extra margin.

For example, a 10-foot published bridge with source MHW 4 feet above source MLLW and a 2-foot predicted tide has an estimated 12 feet of clearance. An 11-foot boat with a 2-foot margin needs 13 feet, so an opening is indicated. At this example crossing, the source tide would need to be 1 foot MLLW or lower for an estimated closed pass with that margin.

Higher water reduces clearance. Lower water can help overhead clearance while making shallow sections worse, so the departure comparison checks fixed bridges as well as priority tide locations. The margin is your adjustable extra headroom; it does not guarantee actual clearance.

Nearby tide sources, clearly labeled

Bridge estimates use a supported NOAA harmonic tide source with published MHW and MLLW values from the same station. Sources are Cape May (8536110), Stone Harbor (8535581), Longport (8534836), Atlantic City (8534720), and Barnegat Inlet (8533615). The source, distance from bridge and datum difference appear in the bridge inspection panel. They are nearby-station proxies, not measurements at the bridge. Local tidal phase/range, wind-driven levels, waves, boat motion, equipment configuration and temporary obstructions can change actual clearance. Barnegat Inlet is particularly a broad proxy for Manahawkin Bay, where local tide behavior differs.

How recorded speed & tide estimates work

The inside passage combines a timestamped August 29, 2022 track from Canyon Club in Cape May with the inside portion of a July 18, 2025 track north to Manasquan Inlet. The Dillon’s Creek marina detour is removed, using a short smooth main-channel connector south of Route 37. Stops include Lavallette and Bay Head at the canal entrance. These are passage points rather than marina approaches. The connector was checked against NOAA chart land polygons; depths were not validated. Obvious stationary time at the start and finish and bridge-area holds were removed. The cleaned moving pattern is reused in reverse for southbound trips.

Open-water sections scale from the 26-knot reference cruise. Slower sections retain their recorded timing as a proxy for restricted or no-wake travel; increasing cruise speed does not make those sections run faster. A lower cruise speed also limits them when it is below their inferred speed. These sections are inferred from recorded progress, not a verified map of legally designated no-wake boundaries. Actual restrictions and conditions take precedence.

Bridge waits are added after the cleaned moving timing; height determines which movable bridges need a wait. Planned stops, docking, refueling and marina detours are not added. The Account for Point Pleasant Canal current checkbox is on by default. In that canal only, NOAA ACT3996 north-bridge predictions adjust speed over ground in either direction at the evolving arrival time, including earlier bridge waits. The adjustable default of 6.1 knots through water comes from the recorded July 18, 2025 speed with its predicted current removed. A lower open-water cruise also limits canal speed. Uncheck it to retain the recorded GPX timing. This applies one current station along the canal; wind, local differences and currents elsewhere on the NJ track are not modeled. Inspect a canal point to see the along-route current and estimated speed over ground.

Saved NOAA high and low tide events supply times and heights. Between those events, a smooth cosine curve estimates the height. At a checkpoint, the selected source is evaluated at that checkpoint’s arrival. Along-route color blends nearby source heights at the same time. Neither is a live observed water level.

Weather along the trip & largest forecast seas

Open Trip briefing on either planner to see temperature, wind, gust and precipitation-chance ranges along the selected passage. Forecasts are sampled at multiple route positions and the times the boat is expected to be there, from departure through arrival. The tide planner uses the whole selected route, including its inside and ocean portions, instead of a single midpoint forecast. Changing departure, direction, endpoints, speed or bridge waits refreshes the forecast for the new timing.

The ranges use available Open-Meteo hourly forecasts at up to 24 route-time samples, with more samples for longer passages. Significant conditions such as strong winds, rain or larger seas are listed with nearby named places, coordinates and estimated encounter times. These are sampled ranges, not a continuous forecast for every point along the course.

Largest forecast seas identifies the highest available significant wave height among the marine route samples, in feet, with the nearest named location, coordinates and estimated time in Eastern time. A significant wave height describes roughly the average height of the highest third of waves; individual waves can be higher. The reported maximum is an estimate among the sampled points, not a guaranteed upper limit. Conditions between samples can differ.

The tide planner requests marine wave data only for an actual ocean portion of the selected passage. For an entirely inside passage it reports that bay and canal waves are not modeled, rather than substituting offshore wave heights. Marine models may not resolve sheltered harbors, narrow channels, inlet effects or local wind waves. Regional NWS sea descriptions remain on the ocean-route options and describe the departure forecast; they are separate from the route-time estimate.

The compact weather summary under Passage options shows the useful ranges and seas estimate, with a short warning if forecasts are incomplete. The trip briefing keeps the detailed location notes and separate weather/marine coverage counts. A failed weather request does not hide an available sea forecast, and a failed marine request does not hide available weather. Missing sections or dates are labeled incomplete or unavailable. Forecast requests cover approximately the next seven days; the much longer saved NOAA tide/current range does not extend the weather forecast horizon. Missing wave data are not treated as calm seas.

The weather panel refreshes with the selected passage, and the tide planner also checks again every 30 minutes. Forecasts do not change tide/current predictions, bridge schedules, clearance checks, passage speeds or departure rankings. Use current official local and marine forecasts when deciding whether to travel.

Data, time & troubleshooting

Why is the page initially busy?
It loads saved prediction blocks and compares 121 departure times. The current planner can take longer because it simulates the whole passage for every candidate. Wait for the calculation status before changing inputs.
How do input changes update results?
The tide planner automatically recalculates after valid changes, including endpoints, departure date/time, cruise speed, boat information and bridge settings. Low-water alert changes update the flags immediately. Incomplete or out-of-range inputs show a message until corrected; choosing the same start and finish requires a different endpoint. Map zoom and position stay unchanged. The current planner also recalculates automatically after valid input changes and keeps a Calculate passage button for an explicit refresh. Selecting a geographic endpoint pans to it without changing zoom or rotation.
Can I use last month’s date or next year’s date?
Use the saved coverage range shown on the page. The cache keeps four historical weeks and roughly 52 weeks of departure dates, plus an arrival buffer. The scheduled weekly refresh is set for Monday at 2 a.m. Eastern. The displayed refreshed date tells you when the saved data were last updated.
Why is a departure missing or marked unavailable?
It may exceed prediction coverage or, on the current page, fail the forward-progress or 120-hour limit. Missing predictions are not replaced with invented zero currents or tides. Shorten the passage, choose a covered date, or review the speed input.
Why is the chart blank or incomplete?
NOAA chart tiles load separately from the saved predictions. Try Simple coastline or reload when the connection improves. Arrival tables can still work while chart tiles are unavailable.
Is my saved boat information shared?
Cruise speed, draft and height are stored locally in this browser. A different browser or device may have different values. The page does not upload those inputs as part of its calculations.
Does this find a safe depth, route or bridge clearance?
No. The planner compares timing and predicted astronomical conditions on a fixed course. It estimates bridge clearance from published heights and nearby predicted tides, but does not verify actual clearance, today’s channel depths, shoaling, notices, weather or the full operating limits of your vessel. Use current charts and local navigation information for those decisions.

Prediction reference: NOAA CO-OPS data API. More background and the reason this project exists: About BitterRadish passage planners.

Passage planning options

Arrive by searches the 24 hours before an Eastern arrival deadline; otherwise departure suggestions search ±10 hours. Candidates with individual bridge waits of 60 minutes or more, incomplete clearance checks, fixed-bridge conflicts or flagged special-event schedules are excluded. Daylight-only also requires sunrise-to-sunset travel along the passage, checked at five-minute intervals and the finish. Weather forecasts are shown separately; weather and visibility do not change passage timing, daylight checks or departure rankings.

Ocean alternatives cover Absecon–Cape May, Barnegat–Cape May and Barnegat–Absecon in both directions. Choose Ocean via Barnegat ↔ Absecon for a trip between a northern inside stop, such as Toms River, Bay Head or Manasquan, and Atlantic City. It follows the inside route to the Barnegat turnoff, goes outside, enters Absecon and continues inside to your destination; Swap reverses the passage. Approach endpoints identify the actual recorded ICW turnoffs. Bypassed stops between the turnoffs are omitted. The former uses the August 25, 2022 track. The Barnegat alternatives use the outbound August 22, 2026 Barnegat approach, the recorded Cape May approach, and a constructed offshore connector checked against saved NOAA land polygons. Fishing, return and marina branches are excluded. That geometric check is not a depth validation. Inlet currents, wind and waves do not adjust route timing. Weather and sea forecasts are shown separately in the trip briefing. Ocean cruising speed is separate from inside speed. Blue ocean legs have no tide coloring; skipped inside checkpoints and bridges do not affect the trip. The Barnegat–Absecon option retains inside timing, bridges and canal-current checks north and south of the replaced section. Its recorded inlet approaches are joined by a constructed offshore leg checked against saved land polygons; this does not verify depth or inlet conditions. Other inlets are not yet available.

Arrival uncertainty compares the tide at each priority checkpoint over the selected ±15, ±30 or ±60 minutes, including intervening high and low predictions. It is a tide-height sensitivity check, not a simulation of missed bridge openings. The briefing prints selected departure/arrival, route, priority tide, bridge waits, canal adjustment, a shortlist of loaded Coast Guard notices, weather ranges along the passage and the largest available forecast seas with their location and time.

GPX comparison matches timestamped points within 0.15 nautical mile of the selected route in two-nautical-mile sections. Sections containing bridge crossings, the canal, pauses, gaps, backtracking, insufficient matching track or large timing differences are excluded from personal adjustment. These are heuristic exclusions; review the results. Personal factors are stored in the browser by route and direction and can be reset. They do not create no-wake zones or change shared data. Historical canal-current correction is not inferred.

Submit for review requires an administrator email in the review configuration. It opens an email draft; the user must send it. It does not silently upload a GPX. Until that address is configured the button is disabled; a downloadable review package remains available. Shared changes require administrator review.
